title: Where your treasure is
hookLine: where your treasure is, there will your heart be also (Matthew 6:19–21)
tomorrow: can you judge anyone at all? two readings of 'judge not'.

cards: Someone chips in for a friend's fundraiser and starts checking the total twice a day. Someone buys a ticket to a game and suddenly cares about the score.

Odd, but it often runs this way: the money goes first, and the caring follows. That's the strange detail in today's line, and yesterday's question. Jesus doesn't say your treasure will follow your heart.
He says it the other way around.

teach.b: Here it is in the Sermon on the Mount. "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven."
And then: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Moth and rust: treasure that rots in a closet or a box. But the puzzle is the last line.
The heart doesn't lead. It follows. Put your treasure somewhere, and your heart goes after it.
Matthew tells a story that shows it.
A rich young man comes to Jesus and asks what good thing he must do to have eternal life. He has kept the commandments.
Jesus answers, "go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven." Treasure in heaven, the sermon's own words. And the young man can't.
Matthew says "he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions." His heart was exactly where his treasure was.
So, on this reading, the puzzle has its answer: you can't always choose a feeling, but you can choose where the treasure goes.
That's the teaching Christians take from it: giving isn't only charity; it's how a heart gets turned.
Where the money and time go, the heart is trained to follow. It's one reason giving is treated as a spiritual practice in churches, not just a bill.

how: Christians read Matthew 6:19–21 alongside the story of the rich young man (Matthew 19:16–22); churches teach giving, such as tithing or almsgiving, as a spiritual practice that shapes the heart.

games.q: what does “where your treasure is” mean?
o: a heavenly bank account that saves up your good deeds
where your heart ends up, since it follows what you value
the gold a man buried in a field in a parable of Jesus

games.q: your nephew wants to care about school but feels nothing for it. what would 'where your treasure is' suggest?
o: put real time into one class first; caring tends to follow what you invest in.
wait until he feels passionate, and then the effort will come naturally.
grades are earthly treasure, so he should stop caring about them.
games.why: in the sermon the heart follows the treasure. invest first, and the caring has somewhere to go.

practice: Look at one thing near you that you paid for or worked hard for: your phone, a ring, a shelf of books. Ask it quietly where your heart has been going with it. Let the answer come without arguing with it.
